rv.q: Dogstar deserves credit for its originality, in how it walks a tonal tightrope few could pull off.
Both witty and heart-rending, this Conrad-esque tale delivers laugh-out-loud humour and a startlingly surreal twist.

The comic timing and delivery was very good, with elder seaman Babben (Justin Edwards) possessing excellent stage presence, even with the character’s gammy leg. There were some good punchlines which had much of the audience, including me, chortling away.

Sam is anxious to please and feels most secure when he can stick to the rules, while Gorey is more mutinous and overtly critical of the Captain’s fatal decisions, which have more than a salty whiff of Moby Dick and Lord Jim .
DOGSTAR is a quirky oddity with a few flaws but surprising charm.
An engaging, thought-provoking and powerful human drama.
Daisy Hall is an author of promise who is well served by cast and director of this fascinating glimpse into nineteenth century whaling life.

What starts out as a psychological drama, with sharp splinters of comedy, becomes a supernatural tale that leaves us all a bit at sea. Describing her writing, Hall recently said in an interview that she sometimes ‘puts people in situations and works out what the play is about later’.

cn.t: Hall's dark comedy about 19th-century whalers trapped in Arctic ice delivers sardonic humor and a surreal twist, though critics remain somewhat divided on its execution. The intimate human drama resonates more than its environmental allegory.
